content: Ammonia is a chemical compound with the molecular formula NH3, typically encountered as a gas with a distinct, pungent odor. While it plays a critical role in meeting the nutritional needs of the planet, ammonia gas is highly caustic and poses significant health risks. a 15-minute limit of 35 parts per million (ppm) and an 8-hour limit of 25 ppm in environmental air. Although ammonia is classified as a non-flammable gas in the United States, it is toxic when inhaled and requires a hazardous safety permit for transportation in quantities exceeding 13,248 liters (3,500 gallons). Commercially, ammonia is often referred to as anhydrous ammonia, emphasizing its water-free state. Despite this, its high heat of vaporization allows it to be handled in standard laboratory equipment, such as beakers, within a fume hood. Household ammonia, also known as ammonium hydroxide, is a solution of ammonia in water.5°C) being the typical high-concentration commercial product. Household ammonia solutions generally range from 5% to 10% ammonia by weight. The ammonia molecule has a trigonal pyramidal geometry, as predicted by Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory. The nitrogen atom in ammonia possesses a lone pair of electrons, enabling the molecule to act as a base by accepting protons. This molecular structure gives ammonia a dipole moment, making it polar and highly soluble in water. In aqueous solutions, a small fraction of ammonia molecules are converted into ammonium ions (NH4+), a process that increases as the pH of the solution decreases. At physiological pH (~7), approximately 99% of ammonia molecules are protonated. Temperature and salinity also influence the proportion of ammonium ions in solution. The ammonium ion (NH4+) has a tetrahedral geometry. Ammonia is widely used in the production of fertilizers, explosives, and organonitrogen compounds. It is also the active ingredient in many household glass cleaners. Ammonia is naturally present in small amounts in the atmosphere, where it is produced by the decomposition of nitrogenous organic matter. Ammonia and its salts are also found in rainwater, volcanic regions, and guano deposits. In biological systems, the kidneys secrete ammonia to neutralize excess acid, and ammonium salts are distributed in fertile soils and seawater. Historically, ammonia salts have been known since ancient times. The term Hammoniacus sal appears in the writings of Pliny the Elder, though its exact identity is unclear. In the Middle Ages, ammonia was used by dyers to modify the color of vegetable dyes, often derived from fermented urine. In the 15th century, Basilius Valentinus demonstrated that ammonia could be obtained by reacting alkalis with sal-ammoniac. Later, ammonia was produced by distilling animal hoofs and horns, with the resulting carbonate neutralized by hydrochloric acid to yield spirit of hartshorn. Gaseous ammonia was first isolated by Joseph Priestley in 1774, who referred to it as alkaline air. Its chemical composition was determined by Claude Louis Berthollet in 1785. The industrial production of ammonia via the Haber-Bosch process was developed by Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch in the early 20th century, revolutionizing its availability and use, particularly during World War I for the production of explosives. Ammonia is one of the most extensively produced inorganic chemicals globally, with production reaching 109 million metric tons in 2004. The largest producers include China, India, Russia, and the United States. Approximately 80% of ammonia production is used for agricultural fertilizers. Historically, ammonia was obtained from the dry distillation of nitrogenous organic waste, coal, or ammonium salts. Modern production typically involves the catalytic conversion of natural gas (methane) or other hydrocarbons into hydrogen, which is then reacted with nitrogen from the air to produce ammonia via the Haber-Bosch process. In biological systems, ammonia is produced by nitrogen-fixing bacteria and through the deamination of amino acids. In humans, ammonia is rapidly converted to urea in the liver via the urea cycle, as ammonia is toxic at high concentrations. Liver dysfunction or genetic defects in the urea cycle can lead to hyperammonemia, which contributes to neurological symptoms such as confusion, coma, and encephalopathy. Ammonia also plays a role in maintaining acid-base balance in the body by facilitating the excretion of hydrogen ions in the urine. Ammonia is a colorless gas with a pungent odor, lighter than air, and highly soluble in water. It liquefies at -33.3°C and solidifies at -77.7°C. Liquid ammonia has strong ionizing properties and is miscible with water. It is a weak fuel and does not readily burn, except in specific air-to-fuel ratios. Ammonia reacts with acids to form ammonium salts and can act as a weak acid under certain conditions, forming amide ions (NH2−). It also participates in nucleophilic substitution reactions, forming amines and amides. Ammonia can replace hydrogen with metals, forming compounds such as magnesium nitride and sodamide. Ammonia serves as a ligand in coordination chemistry, forming complexes with transition metals. These complexes, such as tetraamminecopper(II) and diamminesilver(I), exhibit unique properties and have been studied extensively. Ammonia is also used industrially in the production of nitric acid, fertilizers, and as a refrigerant. It has been employed as a fuel in specialized applications, such as rocket propulsion, and as an additive in cigarettes to enhance nicotine delivery. Ammonia is essential for nitrogen metabolism in living organisms and plays a role in both normal physiology and disease. It is toxic to aquatic life and must be carefully managed in industrial and household settings. Ammonia solutions are commonly used as cleaning agents but should not be mixed with chlorine-containing products due to the risk of forming toxic compounds. Anhydrous ammonia is classified as toxic and flammable, requiring careful handling and storage. It is also used in laboratory settings as a solvent and reducing agent. In interstellar space, ammonia has been detected in molecular clouds and the atmospheres of gas giants, providing valuable insights into the chemistry of the universe. Its unique properties make it a subject of ongoing scientific study, both on Earth and beyond.
